name: Hurghada Marina

notes: Yacht harbour with a promenade of cafes and the departure point for boat trips.

text.description:
Hurghada Marina is a harbour on the Red Sea coast where yachts and dive boats moor, and it is one of the easiest places in town to get a clean, simple photo on a phone. The yachts sit moored in the inner harbour, and their hulls and masts make tidy shapes in the foreground. Beyond them there is open water, so the picture has a clear sense of depth without much clutter. Dive boats also moor here, which adds a bit of local character.

The phone icon on the map is at the marina itself, looking out across the inner harbour toward the open sea. Stand at the water's edge and let the nearest boats fill the bottom of the frame, with the sea and sky above them. Keep the phone level using the gridlines, so the horizon stays straight.

A photography guide recommends early morning, when the water is still and the light is soft. Evening is also worth a visit for reflections and atmosphere, and the lit promenade along the Marina Boulevard helps frame the scene at dusk. If the boats are busy or people walk through, wait a moment and take a few shots rather than just one. Boats move gently, so check each photo is sharp before you walk on.
text.geographic_location: Hurghada Marina is on the Hurghada waterfront, on the Red Sea coast, where yachts and dive boats moor in the harbour. The Marina Boulevard promenade runs alongside it.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot, so start from central Hurghada and navigate to Hurghada Marina using the map. The phone icon on the map is right at the marina, so there is no extra walk once you arrive. Look for the inner harbour with the moored yachts, then use the map's phone icon to find the exact spot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the moored yachts with open water beyond them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the harbour and sky, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out one boat or a detail of its rigging.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The photo shows the moored yachts as clean foreground shapes with open water beyond them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the nearest yachts along the bottom of the frame and the sea and sky above. Use the gridlines to keep the horizon level. For a different view, try Hurghada Marina Boulevard, which shows yachts and dive boats with the Red Sea behind, and the lit promenade framing the scene at dusk.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the nearest yacht to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. At dusk, try night mode, and hold the phone steady against a rail or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the water is still and the light is soft. Evening is a good second choice for reflections and atmosphere.

text.access_note: The harbour area is free to visit. Shooting from the upper floors of marina restaurants would need staff permission.
claims_not_in_sources: Hurghada Marina is a harbour on the Red Sea coast of Hurghada.
Navigating to the marina from central Hurghada using the map is a practical way to reach it.

name: Hurghada Grand Aquarium
label: Grand Aquarium
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q28419476: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Large aquarium with a walk-through tunnel and Red Sea marine life.

text.description:
Hurghada Grand Aquarium opened in January 2015 in the Magawish area of Hurghada. It is Egypt's largest aquarium and one of the biggest in Africa, with nearly 3,500 cubic metres of tank space. Inside there are 24 separate exhibits and more than 1,200 animals from about 100 species. Highlights include a shark tunnel, a rainforest area and 'Whale Valley', which is based on fossils found in the Western Desert. There is also a Bedouin life exhibit and an animal zoo.

It photographs well because there is so much variety. You can get nurse sharks, stingrays, eagle rays and green sea turtles gliding past, as well as birds such as flamingos and pelicans. The shark tunnel is a highlight of the aquarium.

For practical advice, keep the phone close to the glass, which cuts down reflections. Wait for an animal to swim into a clear patch of water rather than chasing it. Take a few frames in a row, because fish move quickly and the first one is often blurred. Wipe the lens before you start, as handling and humid air can leave it smeary. Move at a relaxed pace and let the busier groups pass before you take your shot.
text.geographic_location: The aquarium is in the Magawish area of Hurghada, Egypt.
text.directions_text: Check local transport options for reaching the Magawish area of Hurghada from wherever you are staying. Search for 'Hurghada Grand Aquarium' in your phone's map app. Once there, the phone icon on the map is at the aquarium itself, so there is no further walk to the subject. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most tanks. Try ultra-wide (0.5x) in the shark tunnel if space is tight. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for a single turtle, ray or bird, but only if the animal is close to the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Inside, press the phone gently against the glass of a larger tank.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: In the tunnel, hold the phone level and use the gridlines, with a shark or ray in the upper third. At the larger tanks, fill the frame with water so the animal stands out. Where animals are kept in the open, frame them against a plain background and turn on Live Photos to catch small movements.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the animal to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the water looks washed out. If the lighting is dim, try night mode, but hold very still because moving fish will blur. Take several shots in a row to get a sharp one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a quieter part of the day if you can, so you have room at the glass. For any animals kept in the open, morning is usually more comfortable for you and more active for them.

text.access_note: This is an attraction, so check the official site before you go for entry rules and photography rules.

text.description: Senzo Mall is a modern shopping centre on Safaga Road in Hurghada 1, and it makes an easy, relaxed stop for a casual photo. The main reason to take a picture here is the building itself. Its modern frontage works well as a backdrop for a holiday snapshot of you, your group or the day out. There is no grand viewpoint to hunt for: the phone icon on the map is at the mall itself, and the mall's frontage is the backdrop. The main entrance may not be exactly at the phone icon on the map, so look for the main frontage when you arrive and stand where you get the best view of it. The mall also has an outdoor area called Senzo Avenue, which is used for events. Keep the shot simple. Start with a wide view that shows as much of the frontage as you can, then take a closer one of the details or the people in front of it. Look at the frontage when you arrive and pick the angle that gives you the cleanest background, with the fewest cars and passers-by in the way. If you plan to go inside, check the mall's public Facebook page or confirm locally before you go.
text.geographic_location: Senzo Mall is in the Hurghada 1 district, on Safaga Road. The photo spot is at the mall itself, with its frontage as the backdrop.
text.directions_text: Head for Safaga Road in the Hurghada 1 district and ask for Senzo Mall by name. The phone icon on the map is at the mall itself, so there is little or no extra walk once you arrive. Look for the main frontage when you get there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the frontage. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit the whole front in the frame. Use 2x telephoto for details of the facade or for a neater shot of people with less background.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Check the exact position on arrival and step back from the building to get more of it in the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line them up with the edges of the building so the vertical lines stay straight. Hold the phone level, as tilting it up makes the walls lean inwards. For a group or portrait shot, put people to one side and let the facade fill the rest of the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or the bright walls look washed out. Portrait mode is fine for a single person, but for a group the normal photo mode is safer.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is simplest for a clear view of the frontage. In the evening, check how the building looks and use night mode if it is dim.

text.access_note: The frontage is outside a shopping centre, but check on the ground for any restrictions before you take photos.

name: Al Mina Mosque
label: Al Mina Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hurghada Marina' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'The Bay Hotel Hurghada Marina' (node/11341790570): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W318284617 (Al Mina Mosque): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The main white mosque of Hurghada, with slender minarets near the old harbour.

text.description: Al Mina Mosque is one of the most photographed sights in Hurghada, and the easiest way to see why is to look at it across the water from the marina. From the marina promenade you get the white domes and twin minarets with the Red Sea and moored yachts behind them. That gives you a layered picture with the mosque as the clear main subject. Late afternoon into sunset is the time guides recommend, when the light is warm and the marina is at its most atmospheric. After dark the minarets are lit and stand out well against the water. There is also a second spot at the end of the marina, by the fish market on the map, which gives a closer, more head-on view with fishing boats and water in the foreground. If you only have time for one, start on the promenade for the wider scene and walk on if you want something tighter. You don't need to go inside the mosque to get the picture. Visitors who do go in are expected to dress modestly. On a phone, the key is keeping the minarets upright and leaving a little water or boats in the frame so the mosque has some context.
text.geographic_location: Al Mina Mosque is in Hurghada and is best seen from the Hurghada Marina promenade, looking across the water.
text.directions_text: There is no public transport data for this spot, so use the map to navigate to Hurghada Marina and head for the marina promenade. For the closer view, walk to the end of the marina by the fish market shown on the map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the mosque, water and yachts together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the domes and minarets. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and want the whole waterfront, as it makes the mosque look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hurghada Marina (marina promenade facing the mosque across the water, sunset side). The mosque's white domes and twin minarets, backed by the Red Sea and moored yachts, with the sun setting behind the mosque. On the marina promenade facing the mosque across the water. The mosque lies to the north-east of you. From here the photo shows the white domes and twin minarets, with the Red Sea and moored yachts behind them. For a closer, more head-on view, walk to the marina's end by the fish market, where you can put fishing boats and water in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a minaret up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean. Leave some water and a few yachts in the lower part of the frame. Try one wide shot from the promenade and one tighter telephoto shot of the domes and minarets.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mosque to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the white walls keep their detail and the sky stays rich. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a rail or your body so the lit minarets stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset, and again after dark when the mosque is illuminated.

text.access_note: The marina promenade is a public waterfront space, free to walk according to one guide; the mosque itself expects modest clothing from visitors, and you can check the official site or local information before you go.

The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) makes distant buildings look smaller in the frame.
Holding a phone against a rail or your body helps keep night-mode shots sharp.

text.description: Saint Shenouda Coptic Orthodox Church stands in El Dahar, the old part of Hurghada, and is dedicated to Saint Shenouda. From the outside it looks fairly modest, but the light-coloured walls and large windows give it a calm, dignified face, and the street-front view is the one exterior angle worth a quick photo. Most visitors find the interior more striking than the outside, so think of this as a short, easy stop rather than a long photo session. Stand directly in front of the entrance on El-Lewaa Salman Mazhar Street and take the whole facade from the front. Keep the phone level and use the gridlines so the walls and windows stay straight. If a car or passer-by crosses the frame, wait a moment and try again. This is a working place of worship, so be discreet: ask before photographing anyone, and do not use flash during services. There may be a security checkpoint at the entrance, which is normal. Opening times can change, so check before you go. If you walk up from El-Dahar Square, the church comes into view on the right-hand side of the street, which makes a nice second photo of the approach.
text.geographic_location: In the El Dahar neighbourhood, the old town of Hurghada, on El-Lewaa Salman Mazhar Street.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so head for El Dahar, the old town of Hurghada. If you are on foot in the area, a pleasant approach is from El-Dahar Square, with the church appearing on the right-hand side of the street. The phone icon on the map is right at the church entrance, so there is no extra walking once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straight, natural view of the facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is narrow and you cannot fit the whole building in. Use telephoto (2x or more) only for details such as the windows or the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you are looking straight at the street-facing exterior, with the large windows and light-coloured walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the church up so the vertical edges of the walls match the vertical lines. Keep the phone upright and level to avoid leaning walls. The ultra-wide lens tilts the walls inwards if you angle the phone up, so hold it straight. For a second photo, walk from El-Dahar Square toward the church and photograph it as it appears on the right of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or pale walls look washed out. If you go inside, turn the flash off and keep the phone discreet.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the street is quieter, according to one guide.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so be discreet with photos and check opening times before you go.
